## Packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

## Motivating Question

I want to investigate the relationship between flipper length (y), and bill length (x) (penguins data set)

-- Create summary statistics

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), # this is the more intentional way of 
         !is.na(bill_length_mm)) # filtering for NA values

penguins <- penguins |> # this way is more dangerous
  drop_na() # and removes all rows where one col has a NA
  

penguins |>
  summarise(mean_fl = mean(flipper_length_mm , na.rm = T),
            mean_bl = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = T),
            cor = cor(flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm, use = "complete"))

# cor does not have a na.rm = argument; that is the var function!
# we need to use "complete" to remove NA values (if our data set has NA values)
```

r = 0.653

-- Strength (Moderate/Strong)

-- Direction (Positive)

... of some **linear** relationship

-- Create a plot to investigate our research question

```{r}
penguins |>
  ggplot(
    aes(y = flipper_length_mm, x = bill_length_mm)
  ) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F)
```

## Regression

```{r}
m1 <- lm(flipper_length_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins)
summary(m1)

residuals(m1) |> 
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(id = 1:nrow(penguins)) |>
  arrange(desc(value)) |>
  slice(1,nrow(penguins))
# Goal: report the largset positive and largest negative residual with the obs
```

$\hat{\text{flipper length}} = 127.33 + 1.67*\text{bill length}$

For a 1 mm increase in bill length, we estimate **the mean** of flipper length to increase by 1.67mm.

```{r}
#| echo: true
a <- predict(m1, newdata = data.frame(bill_length_mm = 40))
```

$\hat{\text{flipper length}} = 127.33 + 1.67*\text{40}$

The estimated mean flipper length when bill length is 40mm is equal to `r round(a, 2)`.

## Statistical Inference

$Ho: \beta_1 = 0$

$Ha: \beta_1 \neq 0$

#### Assumptions

-- independence

Comes down to how we sample! Collect data through a simple random sample.

```{r}
plot(m1, which = 1)

plot(m1, which = 2)
```

Note: From our residual vs fitted plot, we don't have strong evidence to reject, the equal variance assumption. Further, we don't see a non-obvious linear trend in our residuals vs fitted (checking for linearity).

Note: We do see some evidence that our assumption of normality is violated, as our Normal Q-Q plot has heavy tails that deviate from the line. However, our sample size is very large, and we are robust to this assumption.

#### The test

```{r}
summary(m1)
```

With a t-statistic of 15.69 and a p-value of \< 0.001 from a t-distribution with 331 degrees of freedom, we reject the null hypothesis that there is no population linear relationship between bill length and flipper length.

## Confidence Intervals

We make confidence intervals to estimate plausible values of our population parameter! In fact, we can create three different confidence intervals depending on our research question:

-- One for $\beta_1$ - population slope

-- $\mu_\text{Y|X}$ - population mean

-- $y$ - individual observation

## Population Slope

```{r}
confint(m1, level = 0.95)
```

## Population Mean

```{r}
predict(
  m1,
  newdata = data.frame(bill_length_mm = 40),
  interval = "confidence",
  level = 0.95
)
```

## Individual Observation

```{r}
predict(
  m1,
  newdata = data.frame(bill_length_mm = 40),
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.95
)
```

Notice how our prediction interval is wider! You knew this mathematically [here](https://st115-fall26.github.io/class/slides/25-reg.html#/prediction-interval-vs-confidence-interval-1)
